title: Introducing Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API
summary: Gemini spark on a space background
story_key: model:gemini|title:introducing tool retrieval in the gemini api
content_excerpt: Tool Retrieval is now in preview in the Gemini Interactions API. Load tool parameter schemas on demand instead of sending your full tool library in every prompt,designed to reduce input tokens and keep tool selection accurate as your agent scales. We are launching Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API to help your agents manage large tool libraries more efficiently. By loading parameter schemas only when needed, you reduce latency and input token costs for complex tasks. You can try this feature today in the Interactions API by adding a tool_search tool and setting defer_loading to true in your requests. We are introducing Tool Retrieval to help developers manage large collections of software tools more efficiently. Instead of loading every tool at once, your agent now keeps a library on standby and only pulls in the specific details it needs for a task. This reduces data usage, speeds up performance, and improves accuracy. You can start using this feature today with our latest Gemini models to build more capable and responsive applications. Today we're launching Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API, available in preview in the Interactions API . When an agent connects to dozens or even hundreds of tools, sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast. It inflates input token counts, adds latency, and lowers tool-selection accuracy as the candidate list grows. Tool Retrieval lets your agent keep its full tool library on standby and load parameter schemas only when the current task needs them. To turn on Tool Retrieval, add a tool_search tool to your request and set defer_loading: true on the tools you want to hold back. The model still sees the name and description of every deferred tool, so it knows what's available, but the parameter schemas stay out of context. When the model needs a tool, it asks for it by name, the API loads the full schema, and the model calls the function, all inside the same request. Inside that single API call, the model searches for issue_refund , the API loads its schema, and the model emits the function_call . All three steps appear in interaction.steps , making it easy to inspect which tools the model considered when debugging tool names or descriptions: From here it's normal function calling: your code runs the refund and sends back a function_result . There's no index to build or host. Gemini runs the search on the server, so the only changes to your code are the new tool and a flag on the tools you want to defer.

title: Introducing object enrichments: Transform unstructured data into agent-ready context
summary:
The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context.

Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a new Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers. Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation.

“L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes.” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal

Agents need context, not raw bytes

To operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges:

  • Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy.

  • Operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems. 

  • Fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted.

This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata.

Key benefits of object enrichments

1. Reduce costs with Google models
Object enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health.

"Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x.” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience

2. Generate richer context with Gemini
For complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

3. No pipeline, low toil setup
Skip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps:

  1. Define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects.

  2. Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs.

  3. Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets.

Object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain.

"Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint

4. Context lives where the bytes live
Instead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context, a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with:

  • Cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs!

  • Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, update, or remove object context.

  • Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences.

  • Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery: You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code.

What customers are building

Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios:

  • Creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents.

  • Automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700.

  • Training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months.

  • Multimodal analytics: Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data.

Get started with object enrichments

Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources

  • Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts.

  • Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data.

  • Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context.

  • Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details.

  • Gemini enrichments: Reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

  • Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

title: LangSmith Tool Gateway: Secure, governed tool use for agents
summary: LangSmith Tool Gateway, now in Public Beta, handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, with policies, approvals, and traces.
story_key: story|title:langsmith tool gateway secure governed tool use for agents
content_excerpt: Agents are moving beyond the chat window to take on more proactive and ambient work. Instead of waiting for a prompt, they run on a schedule or are triggered by events, and they’re handling longer tasks without someone checking every step. That makes them much more useful, but it also means teams need to control which tools each agent can call and whose identity it acts with, and keep a record of every action it takes. Today, we’re launching LangSmith Tool Gateway in Public Beta, on the LangSmith Agent Platform . Tool Gateway is a managed tool layer that handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, making it simple to govern the actions your agents take. Tool Gateway makes it easier and faster for engineering teams to grant agents access to new tools in a controlled manner and without hand-rolling auth each time. Security and compliance teams can use LangSmith to trace and audit tool calls as part of agent monitoring. When agents are in production, platform teams need visibility into what each agent did, controls over which tools and models it can use, and usage policies that limit spend and risk. With LangSmith, developers can build, run, and improve agents in a single platform. LLM Gateway governs the model calls agents make. With it, you can set spend limits and model fallbacks, add rate limits, redact personal data and secrets, and provides visibility within the agent trace with rich information on model calls such as latency, fallbacks, failures, guardrails triggered, etc. Tool Gateway lives in LangSmith alongside LLM Gateway, and provides governance across this lifecycle. Tool Gateway simplifies tool lists for agents, implementing policies on usage, managing identity for tool use, and as with LLM Gateway, provides visibility within the agent trace through rich information on tool calls such as servers, users, outcomes, latency, etc. Together, Tool Gateway and LLM Gateway provide comprehensive visibility and governance over agent actions and spend. Agents in production need to serve hundreds or thousands of users, each with their own set of permissions. This means managing and refreshing a large volume of tokens, and carefully managing and recording access for security and audit requirements. Managing identity and visibility at scale is orders of magnitude more difficult than local development. title: Your Software Factory Needs a Bill of Materials | Daniel Meppiel
summary:
Developers are about to write skills instead of code, and Microsoft's Daniel Meppiel argues the software factory that runs them needs versioning, a bill of materials and signed receipts before enterprises will trust it.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/7jw

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Simon Maple sits down with Daniel, of Microsoft's Global Black Belt team and creator of APM (Agent Package Manager), to dig into why teams keep rebuilding the same skills, how to version a skill when the change is in its behavior rather than a method signature, and why skills can only ever be guidance while security controls stay deterministic. Then stay for Daniel's full DevCon talk, Version Your Factory, Not Just Your Code, on agent contracts, signed receipts and the evidence a regulated enterprise needs before it auto-merges.

What we cover:
– Why developers will write skills and prose instead of code
– Why teams keep rebuilding the same skills, and the case for a shared skill catalog
– Testing and versioning skills with evals: when is a change a major version?
– APM, lock files and an agent bill of materials for your software factory
– Skills are guidance, security controls are deterministic
– Daniel's AI DevCon talk: agent contracts, signed receipts and auto-merging on evidence

title: Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM
summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
story_key: model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast high interactivity decode with flydsl monokernels in vllm
content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. A key design challenge is deciding where a MonoKernel begins and ends : which operations share one launch, and which remain in separate kernels. Fusing more stages is not automatically

title: LangSmith for Coding Agents: Now track spend by outcome
summary: LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce.
story_key: story|title:langsmith for coding agents now track spend by outcome
content_excerpt: Coding is the largest category of enterprise AI application spend, reaching $34B in 2026 . Every company now wants to know what all that spend returns, but most engineering leaders still can’t give an exact answer to what it's buying. To try to understand coding agent ROI, teams used to look at high-level data like usage analytics and AI consumption, but these don’t provide insight into what tokens actually produce. Answering the ROI question is hard and requires visibility into spend across users and teams, along with a way to connect it to outcomes. We felt this friction firsthand when spend with our own coding agent, Robin, started climbing, and is one of the reasons we built a model router. Now we're excited to offer a practical solution for our customers too. LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce. This provides a clearer way to calculate the ROI behind coding agent budgets and understand how changes to models and policies impact it. The new LangSmith Agent Platform operates around the agent. Each agent has its own record and belongs to an "agent type" that determines what its dashboard shows, which data it connects to, and how it's evaluated. Coding agents are the first specialized agent type, and present data on pull requests, one of the signs that the agent's work is useful. LangSmith already traces coding agents across model providers, including Claude Code and Codex . With coding agents in LangSmith, the spend in each trace is automatically attributed to pull requests each agent contributed to. The attribution reflects the tasks a coding agent is used for. It covers both cases where a single thread can open several PRs, and where a PR can take several threads to finish, so data in LangSmith reflects what your agents actually accomplished and what it cost. Up until today, LangSmith enabled you to see the cost per trace for any of your coding agents, one trace at a time. This is useful for manual debugging, but doesn't provide visibility into trends across the entire team. The new coding agent overview page aggregates those costs and ties them to the pull requests your agents worked on. The dashboard shows KPIs at a glance, and clicking any metric opens its trend over time. For example, if your team switched models, you can compare before and after to see the impact of the change. title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
summary: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.

title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
summary: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
summary: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.

title: Four AI Architecture Patterns for Regulated Industries
summary: Enterprise AI cannot replace every deterministic control. These four patterns help...
story_key: story|title:four ai architecture patterns for regulated industries
content_excerpt: How to place determinism, agentic reasoning, human authority and bounded autonomy in enterprise systems Enterprise AI cannot replace every deterministic control. These four patterns help architects decide where agents can reason, act, and remain subject to controls or human authority. Enterprises are adding agents to systems built on fixed rules and repeatable processes. Agents can reason through complex problems, but enterprise systems-especially in regulated industries-must remain controlled and auditable. The question is not which one to choose. It is how to make them work together. We are writing this series because customers ask us the same questions: How are enterprises around the world navigating constraints similar to ours? What is the reality of enterprise AI adoption? How are other organizations approaching these nuances? How is Databricks helping solve them when the requirements are ambiguous, complex, and so specific to the institution? We as Forward Deployed Engineers work at this boundary. We take ambiguous business problems and turn them into production-ready systems. While implementations will vary by institution and we cannot disclose specific implementation details, we can discuss generalized patterns and practices. As agents become part of large enterprise systems, two questions keep recurring: The answer is not the same for every use case. Across the systems we are building and modernizing in the field, four patterns are emerging. This first article introduces the framework. The next four articles show how each pattern works in practice. Use this pattern when outcomes must be strictly deterministic and reproducible, or when errors are irreversible and carry high remediation costs. Here, deterministic means the result can be reproduced under an explicit, versioned contract that records the data, rule, tolerance, configuration, and execution context together. Financial Institutions have lots of controls. Reconciliations are a good example. The control must calculate the balances, apply an approved rule, and produce a reproducible PASS or FAIL. An agent cannot reinterpret the tolerance or turn its own explanation into a passed control. title: BaseRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of a Base Vision-Language Model via Training-Free Harness Internalization
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.

title: claude-code v2.1.327
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a confirmation before /install-github-app changes a repository
  • Added claude mcp add-json <name> - to read the server's JSON from stdin, so tokens can stay off the command line; not available inside a Claude Code session
  • Added a line when a resumed session's earlier messages can't be loaded
  • Added a list in /status of broken agent, skill, command and output style files, keybinding errors, an unavailable sandbox, ignored permission settings and hook matchers that never match
  • Added a note in /config when other settings override a row
  • Added x-claude-code-managed-settings-checksum to the gateway hint headers; sent where managed settings set CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, including where they already do
  • Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
  • Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
  • Remote Control: Fixed stopping the server in worktree mode deleting a running session's git-ignored files, such as .env
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with --use-anthropic-git-proxy deleting a non-empty directory named by GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at startup: the runner now keeps it, ignores the variable and warns
  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content
  • Fixed auto mode ignoring some wildcard PowerShell allow rules that name a script with .\, such as PowerShell(.\scripts\build.ps1 *)
  • Fixed a running Code Mode script in auto mode getting permission prompts and denials once Claude started a second script that auto mode also allowed
  • Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
  • Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
  • Fixed a nested claude with its own token being refused by forceLoginOrgUUID: commands that don't get the session's token no longer get its CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES; set it on any that need it
  • Fixed headless sessions losing stored messages on resume when a message was sent again with the same UUID after the process was killed
  • Fixed cases where a session resumed after an empty reply or a killed command lost an answer, or brought back a rewound prompt, after another crash or a move to the background
  • Fixed a remote session forgetting messages sent after Stop was pressed during a restart, if Claude Code then crashed
  • Fixed tasks created after /clear being lost, and cleared tasks coming back, when a cloud or self-hosted runner session with no feature flags loaded resumed later
  • Fixed a compaction right after a reply cut at the output token limit losing that reply's tool call and its result
  • Fixed a settings change from /config and similar commands failing to save with no warning; a line under the prompt now says so
  • Fixed /rewind closing without a word when some files could not be restored
  • Fixed pasted images being dropped when the prompt starts with a file path such as /tmp/a.txt
  • Fixed agents passed with --agents being lost once plugins loaded or reloaded
  • Fixed a plugin's agent being dropped when resuming a session from the --resume picker
  • Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when https_proxy or HTTPS_PROXY is a bare host:port and neither its input nor its output is a terminal (the desktop app, an SDK, cron)
  • Fixed Claude Code on Linux sometimes returning to the shell while restarting itself at startup, such as after the first sign-in to a Claude apps gateway or when turning on Code Mode
  • Fixed claude -p hanging before its first request when the fetch of a model's settings stalled, such as at a proxy; it now goes on without them after 10 seconds
  • Fixed the screen staying blank or frozen after a brief out-of-memory error
  • Fixed a rare display fault that could freeze the screen or end the session
  • Fixed cloud sessions breaking when a program left thousands of connections open to the session's network proxy
  • Fixed a turn hanging when a mod's $.model.complete or $.model.classify call met a usage limit: the call now gets the API's error at once; mods should handle that error
  • Fixed stalls on a compaction reply with thousands of unclosed tags and on some very long WebFetch URLs; WebFetch now refuses a URL over 2,000 characters before any permission prompt
  • Fixed a message with thousands of @ mentions stalling before Claude replies; only the first 100 mentions are now looked up as files
  • Fixed the prompt freezing after rejecting a write to a very large file; a rejected write now shows a short preview
  • Fixed a crash when a burst of keys reached the search box in /plugin
  • Fixed a false crash report and exit code when a suspended session resumes, or at exit, where a Linux security policy blocks a process from signalling itself
  • Fixed remote MCP servers staying disconnected after a longer outage such as a VPN drop: most servers on other machines reached by hostname over https are now retried in the background for about a day
  • Fixed Edit refusing with "File has not been read yet" after a compaction on unchanged files outside the project that Claude had already read in full
  • Fixed Grep repeating or skipping results when paging with head_limit and offset; content and count results are now sorted by file path

  • Fixed Claude reporting a background agent as still running when it had waited 30 seconds or more on a permission prompt in the desktop app, on the web and in the SDK
  • Fixed Claude not being told in auto mode when a background agent's reply to a follow-up message was dropped, and reduced repeat wake-ups there from agents waiting on background commands
  • Fixed the desktop app, Claude Code on the web and VS Code showing a raw task notification as a subagent's prompt after its background task woke it
  • Fixed messages sent from another session with "later" priority joining the running turn, instead of waiting for it to end, in Remote Control and Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed messages to cloud and Remote Control sessions being reported as failed with a stale address after a timeout or rate limit; Claude now says when a message may have arrived
  • Fixed cloud sessions giving no error when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocks a message sent while Claude works
  • Fixed failing hooks showing nothing: SubagentStop in background agents, SessionEnd at /clear and /resume, and CwdChanged and FileChanged in fullscreen
  • Fixed a Stop hook that failed to run being shown as having reported a problem
  • Fixed focus view keeping a finished reply hidden while a Stop hook was running
  • Fixed Claude getting a long managed PostToolUse hook output twice when a mod added context to the tool call
  • Fixed /model listing the wrong models in some terminal sessions when a project's .claude/settings.json sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an LLM gateway
  • Fixed /statusline writing to ~/.claude/settings.json when CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR points to another folder
  • Fixed claudeMdExcludes patterns on Windows not matching a path whose drive letter is written in the other case
  • Fixed claude agents and claude rm refusing to remove a fully pushed session ("The worktree has unpushed commits") when its worktree has a file or folder named HEAD at the top level
  • Fixed long ListAgents results hiding most sessions on accounts with many cloud or Remote Control sessions: long lists now come in pages
  • Fixed slow turns in resumed sessions for organizations with tens of thousands of connector tool permissions
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed claude -p started by a session's script or hook waiting out rate limits, because it inherited the session's own retry setting
  • Fixed the spend limit menu reporting a changed limit when the server refused it
  • Fixed a second x on a task's details in /tasks stopping the next task too
  • Fixed Esc being ignored on a permission prompt that had just appeared
  • Fixed lists that load their rows late sometimes ignoring Enter and the arrow keys
  • Fixed /autofix-pr holding the keyboard after Esc while it stopped the cloud session; the dialog now closes at once, and a stop that fails is reported afterwards with a link
  • Fixed a blank screen and stray mouse codes in the shell after quitting with ctrl+c just after ← opens the agents view
  • Fixed Ctrl+C right after the trust question leaving the terminal in fullscreen
  • Fixed the shell flashing on screen when ← opens the agents view in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed terminal display faults: most scrambled scrollback in Ghostty on resize, link addresses hidden in Windows Terminal under old tmux and in VTE 0.50.0, and no selection highlight with 16 colors
  • Fixed some garbled rows in tmux with allow-passthrough on inside kitty, Ghostty or iTerm2
  • Fixed /mcp saying no servers were configured after one was added during a session or declined; it now says what to do
  • Fixed /hooks leaving out hooks given by --settings
  • Fixed the / menu listing a row for each skill of the same name, though every row ran the first
  • Fixed /teleport showing no message when the chosen session failed to resume
  • Fixed n and N in transcript search skipping matches
  • Fixed cancelling a transcript search (ctrl+o, then /) in a long session landing far from where the search started
  • Fixed up and down losing the cursor's column over a short or blank line
  • Fixed Tab in shell mode filling in a file name after &&, ; or |, where a command goes
  • Fixed the selected session leaving the screen in claude --resume and /resume when branch names or folder paths are long
  • Fixed the MCP tool list in /mcp and /plugin losing your place when going back from a tool
  • Fixed /resume listing one session fewer than the window has room for, and a 'Resend your message' hint after most spend caps, where resending can't help
  • Fixed an MCP server's long question being cut off after one row, text fields hiding long pastes with no sign, and a doubled divider line in /plugin's options and /login's Bedrock and Vertex steps
  • Fixed the "+N lines" count being too high for command output with links or colors, and the transcript's ? help hiding how to exit in a short window
  • Fixed Ctrl+C twice not closing /chrome from its browser list
  • Fixed a number and Enter typed too early at an agent's plan approval in screen reader mode causing the next number to be dropped too
  • Fixed Claude trying to read design system token files that do not exist when starting a deck or design
  • Fixed exit not saying that a worktree was kept
  • Fixed /hooks help naming input fields that do not exist
  • Fixed question dialogs naming ctrl+g after the external editor key was rebound
  • Fixed two sign-in error messages that pointed to the Claude subscription option on computers where forceLoginMethod is set to console
  • Fixed /config saying the dialog was dismissed instead of "Set theme to …" after changing the theme
  • Bug fixes and reliability improvements

  • Improved narrow terminals: /status, forms and detail screens lay out better, /model and /effort fit at about 40 columns, and key hints such as ←/→ to adjust stay
  • Improved /install-github-app: the repository, secret and API key steps use the standard list and keys, with shorter messages, a spinner and clearer errors

  • Changed Claude in Chrome to refuse uploading some credential files; attach those to the page yourself

  • Changed the Artifact tool to refuse calls once settings turn Artifacts off, in sessions already running too

title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
summary: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three  million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption.
story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices.
